finding: An open review restates the AASM scoring rules: sleep is scored in 30-s epochs, an epoch takes the stage that occupies more than 50% (15 s) of it; W if 50% of the epoch has occipital alpha (8-13 Hz); N1 if at least 50% is low-voltage mixed-frequency 4-7 Hz activity replacing alpha; N2 begins with a K complex or sleep spindle in the first half of an epoch; N3 if slow waves (0.5-2 Hz, 75 uV peak-to-peak on the frontal derivation referenced to the contralateral mastoid) occupy more than 20% (6 s) of the epoch; R if more than 50% of the epoch shows low-voltage mixed-frequency EEG without spindles or K complexes, minimal chin EMG tone and rapid eye movements. quote: the one based on the spectral markers had a low performance (60%) and was not stable in time
caveats: The task file lists article number 046019; the record is 13(2):026019. Window length of the spectral chain is in the paywalled full text.

finding: Neural-network workload classifiers trained on EEG from the same task reached 87.1% (or 85.3% when the training set contained the task), but applied across tasks they fell to 44.8%, with systematic misclassification for some tasks and individuals.
numbers: Within-task 87.1% (same task) and 85.3% (training set containing the task); cross-task average 44.8%; three working-memory tasks at two difficulty levels
baseline: Two difficulty levels per task, within subjects; chance for two classes is 50% (not stated in the abstract)
subjects: Participants with little or no prior exposure to the tasks (count in the full text)
electrodes_band_window: EEG metrics (details in the full text); short task periods

source.authors: Baldwin CL, Penaranda BN
source.title: Adaptive training using an artificial neural network and EEG metrics for within- and cross-task workload classification

evidence_location: Abstract (Europe PMC record 21803164 equivalent; retrieved via title search)
quote: Cross-task classification accuracies were significantly lower (average 44.8%)
caveats: Cross-task here means a different task in the same subject, not cross-subject; full text paywalled.

finding: With small samples, classifiers applied to pure Gaussian noise reach two-class 'accuracies' of 70% or more, so the nominal chance levels of 50% (two classes) or 25% (four classes) understate what counts as above chance; binomial tests or permutation tests give sample-size-aware thresholds.
numbers: Theoretical chance 50% (2-class) and 25% (4-class); empirical decoding of random signals up to 70% or higher in two-class decoding with small sample sets; effects of sample size, class number, cross-validation scheme and classifier type quantified by simulation
baseline: Random Gaussian signals (no true class information)
subjects: Simulations plus MEG and intracranial EEG baseline recordings
electrodes_band_window: n/a (simulation); LDA, naive Bayes and SVM classifiers

source.authors: Combrisson E, Jerbi K
source.title: Exceeding chance level by chance: The caveat of theoretical chance levels in brain signal classification and statistical assessment of decoding accuracy

evidence_location: Abstract (Europe PMC record 25596422)
quote: can yield decoding accuracies of up to 70% or higher in two-class decoding with small sample sets
caveats: The sample sizes at which 70% occurs are in the paywalled full text; Muhl et al. 2014 apply the same binomial reasoning (53.1% threshold for 1,080 trials).

finding: A review of intra- and inter-subject variability in sensorimotor BCIs states that around 15-30% of users cannot produce a task-specific signature robust enough for control, and illustrates how transfer between subjects depends on the pair: 90.36 +/- 5.59% for one subject pair versus 63.21 +/- 8.43% for another.
numbers: 15-30% of users inherently unable to produce a robust task-specific signature; inter-subject transfer accuracies 90.36 +/- 5.59% and 63.21 +/- 8.43% for two different subject pairs
baseline: Motor-imagery classification across sessions and subjects (review of published results)
subjects: Review; the example pairs come from the authors' own prior studies (Saha et al. 2017, 2019)
electrodes_band_window: Sensorimotor rhythms (mu and beta) over motor cortex; details per cited study

source.authors: Saha S, Baumert M
source.title: Intra- and Inter-subject Variability in EEG-Based Sensorimotor Brain Computer Interface: A Review

evidence_location: Section 3.2 'BCI Performance Predictors' (15-30%); Section on inter-subject associativity (subject-pair accuracies) in the Europe PMC full text PMC6985367
quote: Around 15-30% users are inherently unable to produce task-specific signature robust enough
caveats: Published online 24 January 2020 in volume 13 (the 2019 volume; Europe PMC lists the year as 2019). Concerns motor imagery, not the passive mental states of the section; the 15-30% figure is cited from earlier work.

finding: Cross-subject (leave-one-subject-out) emotion recognition from EEG with 18 feature types and an SVM reached at best 59.06% on the DEAP dataset and 83.33% on the SEED dataset.
numbers: DEAP: 59.06% (AUC 0.605); SEED: 83.33% (AUC 0.904); 18 linear and non-linear feature types; SVM; leave-one-subject-out
baseline: Emotion labels of the public datasets; held-out subject never seen in training
subjects: DEAP (32 participants) and SEED (15 participants) public datasets (counts from the datasets, not the abstract)
electrodes_band_window: DEAP 32-channel and SEED 62-channel EEG; features over delta to gamma rhythms; window lengths in the full text

source.authors: Li X, Song D, Zhang P, Zhang Y, Hou Y, Hu B
source.title: Exploring EEG Features in Cross-Subject Emotion Recognition

evidence_location: Abstract (Europe PMC record 29632470 equivalent; open full text PMC5867345 not read)

caveats: Class counts differ between datasets (DEAP tasks are commonly binary, chance 50%; SEED has three classes, chance 33%), so the two figures are not directly comparable; the abstract does not state the class counts.
